newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-MONTGOMERIE COMES HOME FOR BRITISH OPEN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-MONTGOMERIE COMES HOME FOR BRITISH OPEN.

text.p: Colin Montgomerie has come home for the British Open.
In the town where he spent the first five years of his life and where he returned while still in his teens, Montgomerie will carry the hopes of Scotland on the Royal Troon course he played as a boy.
It is the course where his father James has been secretary for the past 11 years.
And it is the Open venue where Montgomerie feels most pressure, though he is trying to avoid that word in the countdown to Thursday's start of the championship.
"To me this is home," he said on Tuesday. "This is where my family are, where my wife is from and my father obviously still works here.
"This is it in major championships for me and it will be until The Open comes back here probably in seven or eight years."

Along with the word "pressure", Montgomerie's recent Open record is a subject he prefers to avoid because it is not good -- four missed halfway cuts in the past five years interrupted only by a joint eighth place at nearby Turnberry in 1994.

This year, after his second place to Ernie Els in last month's U.S. Open and victory with a closing 62 in the Irish Open 10 days ago, Montgomerie has every reason to feel he can finally win his first major title.
"I'm playing possibly the best golf of my 10-year pro career right now and so obviously I'm quite confident about performing better than I have in the past in this tournament.
"There's nothing secret about the fact that I know my way around here and I know what I'm doing on this golf course," the world number four said.
"It's just a matter of going out there and proving it. It's just whether mentally I can cope with the pressure that's been put on."
He is optimistic, he says, because "I'm hitting the ball straight off the tee, my iron shots are quite accurate and I'm actually putting very well right now."
He feels strongly that this Open will be much more than the Tiger Woods Show and that Troon may not suit the young American prodigy as much as Augusta did at the U.S. Masters in April.
Montgomerie was hugely impressed by Woods's 12-shot victory at Augusta, witnessing the American at first hand in the third round when Woods shot 65 to his own 74.
"There is never any substitute for talent and ability and I was privileged to witness it," he said.
"But that course was set up for Tiger Woods and if he doesn't win there at least every second year I'll be surprised.

"But I said let's see what happens at the U.S. Open and if he wins there we would all be in trouble. Now he didn't and that gave us all hope and now this course, with a bit of breeze blowing, doesn't necessarily suit his game either."
Montgomerie's father has some advice on how his son should approach the Open.
"I'll tell him to remain calm and be cool and it will happen," Montgomerie senior said.
"We have a saying 'Keep the head'. That's what I'll tell him."
